Vs.

full_judgment:
S. M. Husain. J.—In this Writ Petition the petitioners have challenged a memo No S3-3/78 dated 14.2.80 issued by the Director General of Bangladesh Post Office causing seniority to one Arun Kumar Sarkei being the respondent No. 4. herein by virtue of a memorandum No. ED/SP-11(M)-9/78-47(50) dated 18th March, 1978 issued by the Secretary, Establishment Division of the Cabinet Secretariat of the Government of Bangladesh providing a comprehensive formula for granting benefits to the employees who participated in the war of liberation, the aforesaid memos have been marked as Annexure 'B' and 'C' to this petition. 

 3. After the issuance of this Rule, respondent No. 1 being the Secretary, Ministry of posts. Telegraphs and Telephones of the Government of Bangladesh entered appearance and filed an affidavit seeking to rely on the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules made on 24th December, 1979, by the President of Bangladesh in exercise of the power conferred under the proviso to Article 133 of the Constitution of Bangladesh for granting antedated seniority to respondent No. 4 over the petitioners. This consequently caused the filing of an application by the petitioners to amend the prayer in the writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979. Thus at present in this writ petition, the only question for decision of this Special Bench is as to whether the aforesaid Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 whereunder the respondent No. 4 was granted antedated seniority over the petitioners under the impugned order Annexure B, has been made in accordance with the provision of the Constitution of Bangladesh particularly with reference to the proviso to Article 133 read with Articles 27 and 29 thereof. 

 4. So far as the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 is concerned, it was issued on 24th December, 1979 by order of the President of Bangladesh with the authentication of the Secretary, Establishment Division in the Cabinet Secretariat of the Government of Bangladesh and it was published in Bangladesh Gazette Extra-ordinary on 24th December, 1979. Rule 2 of the aforesaid Rules says that these Rules shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in any other rules, orders or instructions relating to seniority or other conditions of service of Government servants. Rule 3 has provided exhaustive definition of freedom fighter employed in the erstwhile Government of Pakistan or East Pakistan and subsequently serving under the Government of Bangladesh. In this connection it may be mentioned that the respondent No. 4 was evidently brought by the authority concerned within the category of clause 11 of rule 3 as aforesaid in order to ascribe upon him the status of a freedom fighter. Rule 3(11) says that freedom fighter inter alia means any person being an employee of the Government of Pakistan of East Pakistan on 25th March, 1971 who abstained from duty in the occupation regime and did not receive any salary from that regime with a view to participate in the liberation struggle whether staying inside or outside Bangladesh, for a continuous period of not less than three months immediately preceding 3rd December, 1971 and did not serve under any other government or under any Organisation which was not under the control of the Government of Bangladesh, but could not formally report to the Government of Bangladesh at Mujibnagar. Rule 4 says that a freedom fighter shall be given two years antedated seniority in the post held by him, or in the service he belonged to, on 25th March, 1971 with all attendant benefits in terms of promotion and fixation of pay. Rule 4 has been followed by two examples, first example whereof was however modified by way of an amendment made by the Government on 28th April, 1981 which says that Freedom Fighters appointed in 1960 shall be deemed to have been appointed in 1958 and shall be placed at the bottom of 1958 recruits. Rule 5 says that upon the grant of two years antedated seniority to a Freedom Fighter, his pay shall be refixed having regard to such seniority, without payment of any arrear pay whatsoever. From the consideration of aforesaid relevant provisions of the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 it appear that only Rule 4 is relevant in order to decide whether such rule is warranted under the proviso to Article 133 of the Constitution of Bangladesh and if so whether it is still hit by Article 29 read with Article 27 Of the Constitution of Bangladesh. 

 5. Article 133 of the Constitution of Bangladesh says that subject to the provisions of the Constitution the Parliament may by way regulate the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic provided that it shall be competent for the President to make rules regulating the appointments and conditions of service of such persons until provision in that behalf is made by or under any law, and rule so made shall have effect subject to the provision of any such law. From a careful regarding of Article 133 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, it appears that it has contemplated parallel legislation regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic, either by way of an Act of Parliament or by Rules made by the President. Till an act of parliament is made, the Rules framed by the President as an alternative shall be deemed to be a primary legislation directly made under the Constitution; but once Parliament enacts a law in that regard, the Rules framed by the President shall become secondary subject to the provision of any such law. Admittedly at present Parliament has not as yet enacted any law regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic as contemplated under Article 133 of the Constitution. Thus the Rules made by the President under the proviso to Article 133 of the Constitution regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic including the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 is still a primary legislation for the purpose of determining the constitutional validity thereof. 

 6. Now the question is whether rule 4 of the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 where under two years ante-dated seniority has been granted to all Freedom Fighter employees of the Government can be called to be a rule regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic as contemplated under Article 133 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. This question will have to be considered in the back-ground of the fact that the petitioners and the respondent No. 4, all were employees of erstwhile Government of Pakistan who subsequently joined the Government of Bangladesh. So far as the position of such employees of Government of Bangladesh who were also earlier employees of the erstwhile Government of Pakistan is concerned such persons did undergo a transitional stage whose position has been amply mentioned in paragraph 10 of 4th Schedule of the Constitution of Bangladesh. Although under clauses (a) and (b) of sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule to Constitution, the continuity of the service of such persons on the same terms and conditions as were applicable to them before the commencement of the Constitution, has been fully protected, clause ( b) of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule to the Constitution, however, enables the Legislature to make law varying or revoking the conditions of service of persons employed before the commencement of the Constitution. Thus it would appear that the power to vary or revoke the conditions of service of persons employed before the commencement of the Constitution can only be done by making a law in that regard. Article 133 of the Constitution makes a clear distinction between a law regulating the appointment and conditions of service and Rules made by the President till such law is made. The law referred to in Article 133 of the Constitution evidently means an Act of Parliament. Considering the provision of clause (b) of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution along with Article 133 thereof, it appears that whereas any law made under clause (b) of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution may have both prospective and retrospective effect since it involve persons who were in the service of erstwhile Government of Pakistan, whereas any law made under Article 133 of the Constitution can have only prospective effect since it attempts to regulate the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Government of Bangladesh only. Clause (b) of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution empowers the Legislature to make any law varying or revoking the conditions of service of persons employed at any time before the commencement of the Constitution meaning those who had served under Government of Pakistan and East Pakistan, whereas Article 133 empowers the Parliament and the President to make law and rules regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic meaning those who served only under Government of Bangladesh. A clear distinction must be made between conditions of service of persons employed before the commencement of the Constitution including those who served under the Government of Pakistan and appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Government of Bangladesh only The first one can have both prospective and retrospective effect whereas the second one can have prospective effect only when conditions of service is preceded by an appointment of service, any law or rule regulating such appointment and conditions of service can only mean such conditions of service which are related to the appointment in service which can have only a prospective effect. In this connection reference may be made 6 Article 136 of the Constitution where under conditions of service of any person employed in the service of the Republic may be varied or revoked by law. This power to vary or revoke any conditions of service of any person employ in the service of the Republic by any law under Article 136 of the Constitution may have also both prospective and retrospective effect since it does not tag conditions of service with the appointment of service as contemplated in Article 133 of the Constitution. 

 7. Even if it is assumed that condition of service may be varied or revoked by any law in the nature of any legislative enactment by way of any Parliamentary Act or Presidential Ordinance with regard to any persons in the service of the Republic either under clause (b) of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution or Art. 136 thereof, it is to be considered whether granting two years ante-dated notional seniority by a legal fiction as has been made in Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 can be deemed to be varying or revoking any conditions of service as such. Although conditions of service as such has not been exhaustively defined anywhere in the Constitution, it would appear from clause (b) of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution that conditions of service includes remuneration leave, pension rights and rights relating the disciplinary matters. Fixing of seniority as such has not been specifically included as a condition of service. Seniority in service means a factual state of affairs meaning actual length of service which cannot be determined by a legal fiction as a person's length of age cannot be determined by a legal fiction. 

 8. In view of the discussions made herein before it clearly appears-that with regard to such persons in service of the Government of Bangladesh who were already in service before the commencement of this Constitution even under the Government of Pakistan, the conditions of service thereof may be revoked or varied by or under any lay pursuant of the provisions of clause (b) of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution and Article 136 thereof, having both prospective and retrospective effect. So far as any law by way of an Act of Parliament or Rules made by the President under Article 133 of the Constitution is concerned, such Act or Rules only relate to regulating appointment and conditions of service of persons exclusively in the service of the Government of Bangladesh only having a prospective effect. The Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 include only such persons who were in the service of the Government of Pakistan and participated in the war of liberation of Bangladesh; these Rules by them-selves do not regulate the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Government of Bangladesh as contemplated under Article 133 of the Constitution with reference to its proviso. Article 133 of the Constitution of Bangladesh does not contemplate of making any Rules by the President as in the case of Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979. If the Government was at all desirous to make any law providing for granting two years ante-dated notional seniority by legal fiction to such employees of the Government of Bangladesh who were in the service of the Government of Pakistan but participated in the war of liberation of Bangladesh such law if any and at all, could only be made under the general legislative competence by way of Parliamentary Act or Presidential Ordinance under Articles 80 and 93 read with Article 136 and clause (b) of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution, but in any circumstances not under Article 133 of the Constitution. 

 9. Now apart from the aforesaid position, Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 made by the President under Article 133 of the Constitution also confront Articles 27 of the Constitution. Article 27 of the Constitution says that all citizen are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law, Sub-Article (1) of Article 29 of the Constitution says that there shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic. Clauses (a), (b) and (c) to sub-Article (3) of Article 29 of the Constitution have made exhaustive enumeration of certain exceptions with regard to the substantive right of equality of opportunity in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic as contemplated under sub-article (1) of Article 29 of the Constitution. These exceptions mentioned in clause (a), (b) and (c) of sub-article (3) of Article 29 of the Constitution relate to securing adequate representation of any backward section of citizens in the service of the Republic, reserving appointment relating to any religious or denominational institution and reserving for members of one sex any class of employment or office. Considering the clear provision of Article 27 and sub-article (1) of Article 29 read with sub-article (3) thereof, it would clearly appear that the Constitution does not contemplate any kind of division, classification and discrimination whatsoever between any persons in the service of the Republic on the ground of participation in the war of liberation of Bangladesh. The provision for equality of all citizens before law and their entitlement to equal protection of law as provided in Article 27 of the Constitution and further the provision for equality of opportunity for all citizens in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic as provided in Article 29(1) of the Constitution, have not kept any scope for any division, classification or discrimination between citizens on account of their participation in the war of liberation of Bangladesh. The exceptions to such specific provisions of equality as referred to in clauses (a) (b) & (c) of sub-article (3) of Article 29 of the Constitution even do not mention any such category of persons who participated in the war of liberation of Bangladesh. Considering such position as to the citizens' right to equality before law and equal protection of law and equal opportunity in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic as contemplated under Articles 27 & 29(1) of the Constitution, it must be held that the division of persons in the service of the Republic between freedom fighters and non-freedom fighters and granting two years ante-dated national seniority by legal fiction to freedom fighters as made in Government Servants Seniority of Freedom Fighter) Rules, 1979 is not only an unreasonable classification but also highly discriminatory in view of the fact that all persons in the service of the Republic of Bangladesh who could not be included in the definition of freedom fighters made in Rule 3 thereof, have been made juniors to such persons in the service of the Republic who were included in such definition of freedom fighters as aforesaid; this has caused a permanent disadvantage to non-freedom fighters in the service of the Republic for no fault of their own and it has further caused permanent advantage to freedom fighters in the service of the Republic on account of mere chance and accident. In such circumstances it can be said without any hesitation whatsoever that the attempt to grant two years antedated notional seniority by legal fiction to all such persons in the service of the Republic called as freedom fighters as per rules 3 and 4 of Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 has divided and clad fled all persons in the service of the Republic in a highly unreasonable and discriminatory manner and is thus hit by the equality clauses of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. While dealing with the equality clauses of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, reference may also be made to various provisions of the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979, which though provided for an exhaustive definition of a Freedom Fighter in rule 3 thereof, there is no specific provision for any self-executing machinery to select personnel from amongst government servants on the basis of the aforesaid definition of a Freedom Fighter. In the absence of any machinery being set up under the Rules, there is no statutory authority upon whom the obligation lies to select Freedom Fighters from amongst Government servants objectively on the basis of the definition of Freedom Fighter given in rule 3 of the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979. In such circumstances, there is every possibility and probability of such selection being made wrongly in an arbitrary manner by a person without any lawful authority leading to discrimination against innocent Government servants, if not against genuine freedom fighters also. Thus Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 has all the potentiality of leading to highly arbitrary and discriminatory acts on the part of the authority of the Government leading to the violation of the equality clauses of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. 

 10. In this connection it may be mentioned that every notional and patriotic Government has an abiding obligation to grant rewards, benefits and privileges to such of its citizens who participated in the glorious and historic war of liberation and independence including accelerated promotion in service, but under no circumstances causing permanent disadvantage and discrimination against the bulk of other citizens for no fault or offence of their own. Although People's Republic of Bangladesh finally emerged on 16th December, 1971 and its Constitution commenced from 16th December, 1972, during the early days immediately after independence, no law was made by way of any President's Order providing for such kind of antedated seniority to freedom fighters in the service of the Republic A law made in similar manner could have been saved under the Constitution of Bangladesh as has been made under Article 47 thereof as per its first schedule. This not having been done it must be presumed that the founding framers of Constitution and the earliest law makers never intended to make any such highly unreasonable and discriminatory division, classification of persons in the service of the Republic. It is only in early 1978 that by executive orders, memos and circulars such antedated seniority were attempted to be granted to Freedom Fighters in the service of the Government and other statutory authorities which having been struck down by the Supreme Court as having been made without any lawful authority, in late 1979 the present Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules were made by the President purportedly under proviso to Article 133 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. 

 11. Before concluding it may be mentioned that notwithstanding the best effort, no precedent has been made available to this Court which can be compared with the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979.  Consequently there is no judicial decision of the superior courts either in the Sub-continent or any other Commonwealth or Common Law Countries relating to a matters similar to the present dispute. The only decision nearest to the point that is available is a case reported in AIR 1966 (SC) 602 between State of Mysore and others. In this case scope of proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution of India, which is nearly similar to the proviso to Article 133 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, has been discussed in connection with Rule framed thereunder to the effect that persons invalidly retired should be deemed to be validly retired. A Full Bench of the Supreme Court of India unanimously held that such rule was not within the ambit of the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution of India. Proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution of India empowers the President and the Governors to make rules regulating the recruitment and condition of service. A rule made to the effect that persons invalidly retired should be deemed to be validly retired was not a rule regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of such persons. What is actually a regulatory enactment has been explained in a decision of the. Special Bench of the East Pakistan High Court known as the 'Pan Case' reported in (1964) 16 DLR 486 PLD 1965 Dacca 156 in the case of Haji Ghulam Zamin V. A. B. Khandkar, wherein it has been held that any law regulatory in nature involves inherent limitation and no provision of that law can transgress the frontiers of regulatory nature which such law is supposed to be. While attempting to explain the expression "Regu-lation" it has been observed in the aforesaid decision that it is a term which is though incapable of exact definition but is easily understood. Two decisions of the Privy Council in the cases of Municipal Corporation of city of Toronto and Attorney General of Ontario both reported in 1 896 Appeal Cases at pages 88 and 348 were cited in the aforesaid decision of East Pakistan High Court holding that there is always a basic distinction between prohibition or prevention on the one hand and regulation or governance on the other hand. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in its Full Bench decision in the case of Dr. Nurul Islam reported in (1981) 33 DLR (AD) 201 1981 B.L.D (AD) 140 while considering the constitutional validity of a law empowering the Government to cause retirement of any Government servant on the completion of 25 years of service, has held that any law with regard to persons in the service of the Government of Bangladesh who were also in the service of the Government of Pakistan prior to the commencement of the Constitution, varying or revoking their terms and conditions of service as contemplated under clause (b) of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 10 of the 4th Schedule to the Constitution read with Article 150 thereof, must be in conformity with the fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution; it has been further held therein that any law or rule made under Article 133 of the Constitution must be subject to the fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution and thereby section 9(2) of Act XII of 1974 empowering the Government to cause retirement of the Government servants after completion of 25 years of service prior to the completion of the age of superannuation was held to be hit by Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. 

 12. Considering the aforesaid portion it becomes unmistakably clear and conclusively established that Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 with particular reference to rule 4 thereof causing two years ante-dated notional seniority by legal fiction to all employees in the service of the Government of Pakistan and East Pakistan and continuing to serve in the Government of Bangladesh who become freedom fighters as per definition given in Rule 3 as aforesaid being not in the nature of regulating the appointment and conditions of service of persons serving under the Government of Bangladesh, was in any event beyond the scope of Article 133 of the Constitution and is further hit by the equality clauses of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. 

 13. For the foregoing reasons Rule 4 of Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979 is hereby declared to have been made without any lawful authority under Article 133 of the Constitution and is further declared to have been hit by the equality clauses of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution for which such rule must be declared to be void under Article 26 (2) read with Article 7 (2) of the Constitution. Consequently the impugned order passed by the Director General of Bangladesh Post Office being Annexure 'B' to this petition causing ante-dated seniority to respondent No. 4 above the petitioners herein must be held to have been made illegally, without any lawful authority, having no legal effect. This Rule is made absolute accordingly without any order as to costs 

 15. The Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the order dated. 14.2.80 of the Director-General, Bangladesh Post Office, should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority. By that order Arun Kumar Sarker, respondent No. 4, was granted two years ante-dated seniority with all attendant benefits in terms of promotion and fixation of pay in pursuance of Memorandum No. ED/SP-11(M)-9/78-47(500) dated 8th March 1978 of the Cabinet Secretariat, Establishment Division of the Government. 

 16. During the hearing of the Rule before the Division Bench a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition was filed on 20th June, 1981 by the Government, respondent No. 1, stating inter alia that the impugned order was meant to be issued in pursuance of the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules. 1979. Before this Special Bench the petitioners by an application for amendment of their petition, have challenged the vires of the said rules of 1979. 

 18. On behalf of the respondent No. 1 it has been contended that abstention from duty during the war of liberation was a risky thing, and that respondent No. 4 participated in the war of liberation by not serving the Pakistan Government and as such he was entitled to two years ante-dated seniority and other benefits under the rules. 

 19. Before this Special Bench respondent No. 4 filed an affidavit-in opposition on 10-11-81. He asserted that he joined the non-co-operation movement, launched against the Military Government of Pakistan, and refrained from serving the occupation regime till the liberation of Bangladesh He did not draw-his salary during the liberation period. He left Bogra on 18.4.71, when its fall to the Pakistan Army became imminent. During the nine months of the war of liberation he moved from one place to another within Dhunot, Gabtali and Shariakandi Police Stations in the district of Bogra for organising people's resistance. In spite of repeated calls made by the Pakistan Military authority over the radio he did not join his duty. The Government of Pakistan promoted him to the post of Assistant General manager, Postal life Insurance in May, 1971, but he did not accept the promotion. Respondent No. 4 also claimed that his residence at Bogra was set on fire and all his personal effects were looted and burnt by the Pakistani Army. 

 21. From the above report dated 24.8.78 and from his assertions in his affidavit-in-opposition respondent No. 4 appears to be one of the officers who may be regarded as a freedom fighter within the meaning of clause (ii) of Rule 3 of the Government Servants (Seniority of Freedom Fighters) Rules, 1979. No exception can be taken to the Government's decision to extend the benefits under the Rules to respondent No. 4. 

 23. The elected representatives of the country proclaimed independence on 10th April, 1971 at Mujibnagar. By the Laws Continuance Enforcement Order of the same date it was declared "that all Government officials, Civil, Military, Judicial and diplomatic who take the oath of allegiance to Bangladesh shall continue in their offices on terms and conditions of service so long enjoyed by them and that all District Judges and District Magistrates in the territory of Bangladesh and all diplomatic representatives elsewhere shall arrange to administer the oath of allegiance to all Government officials within their jurisdiction." 

 24. Within a few weeks of the victory of the national liberation struggle the Government of Bangladesh (Services) Orders (P.O. No. 9 of 1972) was made on 24th January, 1972 in order to establish an administrative machinery which could effectively meet the urgent tasks of national reconstruction and for necessary administrative reorganisation. For removal of doubt it was clearly provided by Art. 5 of that Order that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law for the time being in force, no person has any claim to employment in the service of or any other claim whatsoever against the Government on the basis of having been employed at any time in the service of Pakistan." This P.O. No. 9 of 1972 was included in the first schedule to the Constitution and given protection under Art. 47 of the Constitution from being challenged on the ground of inconsistency with, or repugnant to, any provision of the Constitution Two days after the promulgation of the 20th August, 1975 that Order of 1972 was repealed by Ordinance No XLIV of 1975 

 (a) derogate from the continued operation of the Government of Bangladesh (Services) Order, 1972 (P.O. No. 9 of 1972), or the Government of Bangladesh (Services Screening) Order, 1972 (P.O. No. 67 of 1972); or 

 27. From the Government Memorandum dated 18th March 1978 (Annexure 'C' to the petition) it appears that a good number of Government servants actively participated in the war of liberation by formally reporting to the Government of Bangladesh at Mujibnagar or by abstaining from official duties under the occupation regime and not drawing their salary in order to participate in the liberation struggle, or by declaring their allegiance to the Government of Bangladesh at Mujibnagar, from abroad. Certain benefits were granted to some of these employees under Memo No. ED(M- 2)220/75-1014(50) dated 22nd May, 1975. 

 28. It appears as long as the President's Order No. 9 of 1972 was holding the field, because of its Art. 5 there was no legal bar for conferring some service benefits like promotion, etc. on a Government servant who participated in the liberation war, as such action could not be challenged by one who was otherwise similarly situated but did not participate in the liberation war as he had no claim whatsoever against the Government on the basis of having been employed in the service of Pakistan. Rule 6 of the impugned Rules indicates that some Government servants were given promotions on account of their participation in the war of liberation. It was only after P.O. No. 9 of 1972 was repealed in 1975 the need for an appropriate frame-work for extending some benefits to the Freedom Fighters was felt, and a comprehensive formula was laid down in the Memorandum dated 18.3.78. Finally, in exercise of the power conferred by the proviso to Art 133 of the Constitution the President, after consultation with the Public Service Commission, made the Rules in order to regulate the matter in accordance with law The Rules were published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 24th December, 1979. 

 33. It has earlier been noted that certain benefits were granted to some government servants who participated in the liberation movement, but the existing rules and practice proved inadequate to cover all relevant cases. For clearly defining the categories of employees who would be entitled to service benefits in recognition of their participation in the liberation struggle as well as to stipulate the benefits the Memorandum dated 18th March, 1978 laid down certain guidelines, and, finally, the impugned Rules were made to regulate the whole matter. Granting of certain service-benefits like two years ante-dated seniority on government servants who attained same distinctions as government servants in the service of, and, for the cause, of the Government of Bangladesh, are matters related to the conditions of service and the President is competent to make Rules in this regard. The impugned Rules do not suffer from any infirmity. 

 35. There is no doubt that a law may be made for varying or revoking the conditions of service of those Government servants like the petitioners whose services were continued under paragraph 10 of the Fourth Schedule, but such law cannot claim immunity from being challenged on the ground of violation of fundamental rights. 

 37. In support of their contention that the Rules are violative of Arts. 27 and 29 of the Constitution, the petitioners have cited a few decisions of the Indian Supreme Court: Ramkrishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar AIR 1958 SC 538, Accountant-General v. N. Bakshi AIR 1962 SC 505, Jatsinghani v. Union of India AIR 1967 SC 1427, State of Mysore v. Krishna Murthy AIR 1973 SC 1146. I do not propose to review those cases. Those are decisions on their own facts. The facts of the present case are totally different. 

 38.  The impugned Rules are directed to certain problems, made manifest by experience, in the service of the Republic, in the years following the liberation war, and in order to sustain the presumption of its constitutionality the court may take into consideration the background of the legislation. The Rules have remedied an anomalous situation where some freedom fighters had already received some benefits as it appears from the Memorandum dated 18th March, 1978 and as it is indicated in Rule 6, and some others could not be granted similar benefits for want of necessary rules. The rules have laid down reasonable guidelines for election or identification of freedom fighters so that certain benefits may be extended uniformly without picking and choosing, to all Government servants who come within rule 3. The differentia laid down in the Rules are reasonable and they flow from actions, abstentions or sufferings of the Government servants in the service of, and for the cause of, the Government of Bangladesh. The Rules have nexus with the purpose of regulation of the conditions of service of the persons who were in the employment of Pakistan, and now, in the service of the Republic. 

 39. Conferment of certain benefits on the Government servants who participated in the liberation struggle, or abstained or defected in favour of the Government of Bangladesh at Mujibnagar or suffered imprisonment, or dismissal or detention in the hands of the occupation army for the cause of the nascent struggling Government of Bangladesh cannot be objected on the ground of alleged violation of Art. 27 of the Constitution by the petitioners who were not similarly circumstanced with the freedom fighters. 

 40. It is not correct to say that the Rules classified alt Government servants into freedom fighters and non-freedom fighters. The impugned Rules affect only those persons who were in the employment of the Government of Pakistan, East Pakistan or West Pakistan on the 25th March. 1971 whose services were continued with a clear constitutional provision that their conditions of service could he altered. The inter se seniority of all other Government employees have been kept intact. 

 I do not also find any force in the contention that the Rules disturbed the petitioners right to be governed under Rule 32E. of the Post and Telegraph Manual Vol- IV in view of the clear provision of rule 2 of the impugned Rules which provides that the rules shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in any other rules, orders or instructions relating to seniority or other conditions of service of Government servants for the time being in force.
